# Nim for Python, Go, and Rust programmers

This book is written for readers who already write programs in another language but have never used
Nim. This page collects the word equivalents and habits for the three languages most often used
alongside Nim: Python, Go, and Rust. There are no examples to run; the focus is mapping the habits
already in place, so the switch feels light. Each part starts from a table of equivalents, then
briefly explains what stays the same and what needs adjusting.

## Variables

| Language | Declaration |
|---|---|
| Python | `x = 1` |
| Go | `var x int = 1`, `x := 1` |
| Rust | `let x = 1;`, `let mut y = 2;` |
| Nim | `var x = 1`, `let y = 2`, `const Z = 3` |

All three infer the type from the initial value, and Nim follows the same habit. The Python habit of
writing `x = 1` with no type still works, while type checking stays as strict as in Go and Rust.
What differs: Nim offers three levels, from `var` that can change freely to `const` computed at
compile time.

## Functions

| Language | Form |
|---|---|
| Python | `def f(a, b=1): return a + b` |
| Go | `func f(a, b int) int { return a + b }` |
| Rust | `fn f(a: i32, b: i32) -> i32 { a + b }` |
| Nim | `proc f(a, b: int): int = a + b` |

Parameter types are written as in Go and Rust, and defaults as in Python. The last expression of a
procedure body becomes the return value, so `return` is rarely needed. Overloading is allowed, so
several procedures may share a name as long as their parameter lists differ; Python and Rust do not
have this, but Java programmers will find it familiar.

## Structs and objects

| Language | Form |
|---|---|
| Python | `class Point` with `__init__` |
| Go | `type Point struct { X int }` |
| Rust | `struct Point { x: i32 }` |
| Nim | `type Point = object` with fields |

Nim separates data from behavior. A method is an ordinary procedure whose first parameter has that
type, called with a dot as in Python. A value object is copied whole on assignment, while a
`ref object` is copied as a pointer. Class inheritance is limited, since Nim leans more on generics and
concepts to compose types.

## Interfaces and concepts

| Language | Form |
|---|---|
| Python | duck typing and `typing.Protocol` |
| Go | `type Shape interface { Area() float64 }` |
| Rust | `trait Shape { fn area(&self) -> f64; }` |
| Nim | `concept`, generic bounds, or the old `interface` |

A Nim concept is not recognized at program runtime; it is checked during overloading at compile
time. That is closer to a Go `interface` than to a Rust `trait`: both are structural, so a type that
happens to have a matching procedure satisfies them with no explicit `impl` as in Rust. A concept
checks the shape of a type, such as the presence of a field or a procedure, without demanding an
inheritance declaration. A type from another library can therefore satisfy it untouched.

## Error handling

| Language | Form |
|---|---|
| Python | `try`/`except`/`raise` for all errors |
| Go | `if err != nil` with multiple return values |
| Rust | `Result[T, E]` and the `?` operator |
| Nim | `try`/`except`/`raise`, the `raises` effect checked by the compiler |

Nim uses exceptions as Python does, but it moves the checking up to compile time. A procedure can
state which exception types may leave it, and the compiler rejects a promise that is broken. An
unhandled error stops the program with a stack trace, much like Python. The difference is that a
procedure signature can restrict which types may escape, so error handling becomes part of a
readable contract.

## Packages

| Language | Form |
|---|---|
| Python | pip, PyPI, `requirements.txt` |
| Go | Go modules, `go get` |
| Rust | cargo, crates.io, `Cargo.toml` |
| Nim | nimble, the `.nimble` file, `nimble install` |

The role is the same: install and pin the project dependencies. A project usually has a single
`.nimble` file at its root, matching `Cargo.toml` or `go.mod`. Nim also has `nimble.directory` as a
public package index.

## Build

| Language | Form |
|---|---|
| Python | run by the interpreter, with no build step |
| Go | `go build`, `go run` |
| Rust | `cargo build`, `cargo run` |
| Nim | `nim c`, `nim r`, `nimble build` |

Nim translates code to C or C++ and then calls the C compiler. The resulting binary therefore
stands alone, with no language runtime to install alongside it. Another target is picked with
`nim cpp` or `nim js`. During development, `nim r` skips naming the binary and runs the
result right away.

## Testing

| Language | Form |
|---|---|
| Python | `unittest`, `pytest` |
| Go | `go test`, `_test.go` files |
| Rust | `cargo test`, the `#[test]` attribute |
| Nim | `std/unittest`, `suite`, `test`, `check` |

The shape is close to Rust and Go: test blocks live in the same or a separate file, then run by the
compiler as an ordinary program. `check` tests one boolean expression, and `expect` makes sure an
exception is actually raised. Both report failure with a non-zero exit code, so they suit CI.

## Concurrency

| Language | Form |
|---|---|
| Python | `asyncio` with `await`, bounded by the GIL |
| Go | goroutines and channels with `select` |
| Rust | threads with `Send`/`Sync`, `async`/`await` via tokio |
| Nim | `{.async.}` in `std/asyncdispatch`, threads, and `spawn` |

Nim has two tracks: `async`/`await` for IO in one thread, and real threads. Since Nim 2.x threads are
on by default (`compileOption("threads")` is `true`), so `--threads:on` is no longer needed. The
async model uses a single event loop, and tasks wait without blocking the thread. For communication
between threads there is `Channel[T]`; `std/threadpool` and `spawn` still exist but are marked
deprecated. What Nim does not have is Go's goroutine model, lightweight goroutines with `select`
over many channels.

## What is similar

Static types with inference, generics, closures, and modules feel familiar from all three
languages. A procedure can be called in method style, so `text.len` equals `len(text)`. Nim also
offers `let` and `const` as immutable by default, in line with Rust `let` and Go `const`. Functions
are values, so they can be passed and returned. The package manager plays the same role as pip, Go
modules, and cargo.

Beyond that, overloading and default parameter values feel natural to Python writers, while types in
signatures feel natural to Go and Rust writers. Nim knows ranges, slices, and inserting values into
text like a Python f-string, though the syntax differs. Iterating with `for` and counting with `len`
exist in every language, so nothing truly has to be learned twice. Another relief is that common
mistakes such as an off-by-one index or an unclosed block feel similar, so old reflexes still pay
off. Arithmetic and comparison operators are nearly the same, so old expressions can often be
copied with only a small adjustment.

## What is different

Nim compiles to a binary through C, C++, or JavaScript; there is no virtual machine interpreting
code at runtime. Indentation delimits blocks, as in Python, with no curly braces. Memory management
uses ARC or ORC with deterministic destructors, not a stop-the-world garbage collector. `nil` applies
to `ref`, `ptr`, `cstring`, `pointer`, and procedures; value objects are never `nil`. The `raises` effect is
checked by the compiler. The range `0 .. 5` is inclusive, while Python `range` is exclusive. `and`,
`or`, and `not` replace `&&`, `||`, and `!`. There is no built-in `async`/`await` keyword; async is
built with the `{.async.}` macro. Integers have fixed widths, not arbitrary precision as in Python. Overflow of a signed integer
raises `OverflowDefect` even under `-d:release`; unsigned integers wrap; only `-d:danger` disables
that check.

A value object is copied on assignment, not shared through a reference as a Python `class` is. To
share, use a `ref object`. There are no decorators as in Python; pragmas in `{.braces.}` and macros
take over that role. Class inheritance is avoided; generics, concepts, and variant objects are used
more often to compose types.

Nim also does not use the Rust `?` operator to forward errors; exceptions are written explicitly
with `try`/`except`. On the other hand, the exhaustive check on `case` means the compiler often
catches a mismatch before the program runs. The opening and closing braces common in Rust and Go
are replaced by a colon and indentation.

## Pitfalls

Indentation is significant, and tabs may not be used to indent. Mixing spaces and tabs makes the
compiler reject the file or read it wrongly. A `var` parameter lets a procedure mutate the caller
variable with no explicit pointer. Nim identifiers ignore case and underscores except for the
first letter, so `get_name` equals `getName`, but `GetName` differs. `var n: Node` for a
`ref object` holds `nil`, so `new(n)` is needed before use. Copying a `ref` copies the pointer,
not the contents, so two names can point to the same object. A `case` on an enum must be complete,
and the compiler rejects a missing branch. There is no automatic conversion from an `int` variable
to `float`; a literal such as `1` is still accepted. `if` runs while the program runs, whereas
`when` is settled at compile time; swapping them changes the meaning. A string is not a sequence of `char`, and `s[0]` has type `char`. Finally, `echo` adds no
separator between arguments.

If the compiler complains about the `raises` effect, do not rush to turn it off; usually there is an
exception that truly needs handling. `discard` is not idle ceremony either: calling a procedure that
returns a value without using it is rejected, and that catches mistakes easily missed in a dynamic
language. In a variant object, the same field may not appear in two `case` branches, so field names
need careful choosing from the start.

One more thing, type and variable names are told apart by the first letter only; the official Nim
style is `PascalCase` for types and `camelCase` for other names. Keeping one style from the start
avoids a surprise when the compiler treats two different names as the same identifier.

Moving to Nim does not require discarding old habits. What needs adjusting is mainly three things:
indentation that delimits blocks, effects checked by the compiler, and memory management without a
stop-the-world garbage collector.
